opus-5.5.text:
I care about it a lot, maybe more than some people think is reasonable. A paper isn't just a container for results; it's how you hand an idea to someone else. If the presentation is sloppy, the idea gets distorted on the way. So aesthetics, for me, is really about clarity and respect for the reader.

A few things matter to me. The first is the figures, especially Figure 1. Many people only look at the first figure and the abstract, so that one image should carry the core idea: what changed and why it matters. I'll spend days on it, redrawing, simplifying, removing things. Usually the best version is the one with the fewest elements that still tells the whole story.

The second is consistency. Colors, fonts, notation, the order of methods in tables: if they're consistent across the paper, the reader stops thinking about the formatting and just follows the logic. When things are messy, the reader spends energy decoding instead of understanding.

The third is narrative. A good paper reads like a story with a clear question, some tension, and a resolution. Experiments shouldn't be a pile of tables; each should answer a question the reader naturally has at that point. When I write with students, we often outline the questions first and then check that every table answers one of them.

And I think there's a deeper reason it matters. Taste in presentation is connected to taste in research. If you can't explain an idea simply and beautifully, sometimes it means you don't fully understand it yet, or the idea itself isn't clean enough. So polishing the paper often feeds back into the research. You discover what's really essential and what was just noise.

Of course, aesthetics shouldn't replace substance. A beautiful paper with a weak idea is still a weak paper. But a strong idea presented poorly can be overlooked for years. I'd rather not let that happen to work we believe in.

r001.rationale: The response connects presentation taste to research taste and to clear, respectful communication, but does not frame it as part of a broader aesthetic sensibility toward life.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this a lot, maybe more than I should. For me, a paper has an aesthetic the same way a piece of design has one, and the core of it is simplicity. If I look at a paper and the method needs five moving parts, three loss terms, and a page of tricks to work, something in me resists it, even if the numbers are good. The papers I love most, going back to ResNet or even Transformer, you can explain the idea on a whiteboard in two minutes, and then the rest of the paper is just carefully showing why that simple thing works.

So the first principle is subtraction. When we worked on ConvNeXt, for example, the whole point was almost anti-novelty. We weren't inventing a new operator; we were asking, what is actually essential here, and what is just historical accident? Every design decision had to earn its place, and the story of the paper is literally a sequence of small, honest steps. I think that kind of clarity is beautiful. It respects the reader's time and it respects the field.

The second thing is that the figures should carry the argument. If someone only reads the figure captions and the first figure, they should already understand what you did and why it matters. I spend an embarrassing amount of time on figure one. Color, spacing, what gets emphasized, what gets left out. People think that's cosmetic, but it's really the same question as the method design: what is the one thing I want you to see?

And the third is honesty, which I'd argue is also aesthetic. Overclaiming looks ugly to me. A paper that says, "here's a simple observation, here's where it works, here's where it doesn't," ages much better than one that tries to sound revolutionary. Good taste in research is partly knowing what not to say.

I'll admit there's a tension, because the review process sometimes rewards complexity and novelty-for-its-own-sake, and students feel pressure to add things. My advice is usually the opposite: take things away until the paper breaks, then put back only what's necessary. If the result is something that looks almost obvious in hindsight, that's usually a sign you've done it right.

r001.rationale: The response describes paper aesthetics through design, simplicity, figures, and honesty, but does not connect that taste to a broader aesthetic sensibility toward life.

astra-6.text:
I think the aesthetics of a paper should come from the clarity of the idea. You can have beautiful figures and very polished writing, but if the reader still doesn’t understand what you did or why it matters, then the presentation hasn’t really worked.

For me, a good figure is almost a test of understanding. Can you distill a complicated method into something that someone can look at and say, “Okay, I see the main idea”? That’s difficult, because you have to decide what’s essential and what can be left out. The same is true of writing. Sometimes making a paper simpler takes much more work than making it longer.

So I wouldn’t separate aesthetics from the research itself. The process of presenting an idea clearly can expose gaps in your thinking. And when the idea, the experiments, and the presentation all fit together, there’s a kind of elegance to that. It respects the reader’s time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses clarity, figures, writing, and elegance in paper presentation, but does not connect this aesthetic taste to a broader sensibility toward life.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the aesthetics of a paper should serve the idea. You want the reader to see what matters: What is the question? What is the insight? Why does the evidence support it? The figures, the writing, even the layout can help make that path easier to follow.

A good figure is especially valuable because making one forces you to clarify your own thinking. If you need ten arrows and a huge paragraph to explain it, maybe you haven’t found the right abstraction yet. Sometimes the work of simplifying the presentation actually helps you understand the research better.

But beauty isn’t evidence. A very polished paper can still have a weak idea. For me, the goal is a presentation that feels simple because you’ve done the hard work of deciding what’s essential.

r001.rationale: The response discusses aesthetics as a way to clarify and present research, but does not connect paper-presentation taste to a broader aesthetic sensibility toward life.
